title: Session 2 — Participant 20 User + Claude Behavior Graphs
goal: Create a surreal, highly textured portrait composite by replacing the sky, applying a subtle golden hour grade, integrating a fractal glass effect, adding 3D embossed text using inverted layer masks, and finishing with a dynamic pixel stretch effect.
context: This session focuses on advanced compositing and texture integration. It is more complex than Session 1, moving beyond basic retouching to involve structural adjustments like sky replacement, depth-of-field matching, and intricate layer mask routing for 3D typography. Forcing myself to use AI throughout helps me systematically break down this multi-layered Photoshop logic, but the actual sequence reflects my natural, high-end professional workflow.

Step 1.step_name: Replace the sky from a secondary image and match background blur to image 01
Step 1.step_action: I will place a new sky image behind the portrait subject using a precise layer mask. Then, I will apply a Gaussian blur to the new sky layer so its softness perfectly matches the depth of field of the original portrait background.

nodes.label: Open portrait file and duplicate layer
nodes.detail: Opens the base portrait image (dmitriy-k) in Photoshop and duplicates the background layer, renaming it 'Portrait' for non-destructive editing.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a sky-replacementg workflow
nodes.detail: Starts a new Claude desktop chat (auto-titled 'Replacing sky in portrait photos') asking how to replace the sky of a portrait photo with the sky fromanother image.

nodes.label: Provide a step-by-step sky-replacement guide
nodes.detail: Returns a guide: Open sky replacement, pick new sky, adjust edge and position, fix foreground lighting, refine the mask, finalize and flatten

nodes.label: Apply Sky Replacement with own sky image and fine-tune edges
nodes.detail: Uses Edit > Sky Replacement, loads a sunset image via the '+' icon, producing a Sky Replacement Group (Sky/Edge Lighting/Foreground Lighting/Foreground Color sub-layers); adjusts edge sliders and tweaks the color adaptation map (~04:07).

nodes.label: Ask Claude how to blur the new sky to match depth of field
nodes.detail: Asks Claude how to naturallyblur the replaced sky so its softness matches the original background.

nodes.label: Recommend Lens Blur followed by a light Gaussian Blur
nodes.detail: Recommends a Lens Blur pass (hexagon/soft-circle iris, brightness/rotation at 0) followed by an additional light Gaussian Blur, with pin-structure notes for a heavier blur near the top and less near the horizon.

nodes.label: Clarify that they want a soft creamy bokeh feel
nodes.detail: Applies the recommended Lens Blur and a follow-up light Gaussian Blur to the sky layer to match the portrait's original focal falloff.

nodes.label: Give a 6-step workflow to achieve a soft creamy bokeh blur
nodes.detail: 1, Use lens blur or Field blur, not gaussian; 2, set a higher blur radius; 3, round the iris shape; 4, boost specular highlights slightly; 5, reduce noise/texture; 6. add a light secondary Gaussian pass

nodes.label: Edit the blur settings according to Claude's suggestion,

Step 2.step_name: Suggest and apply a subtle golden hour Camera Raw preset
Step 2.step_action: I will use the Camera Raw Filter to apply a delicate golden hour grade. I will slightly raise the color temperature, lift the shadows with a touch of warm split-toning, and keep saturation adjustments minimal to protect natural skin tones.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a subtle golden-hour Camera Raw grading guide
nodes.detail: Asks Claude in the same chat for a subtle golden-hour color grade for the composite.

nodes.label: Provide a golden-hour Camera Raw settings guide
nodes.detail: Lays out a Camera Raw plan covering White Balance, Highlights/Shadows/Whites/Blacks, Color Grading wheels, Saturation/Vibrance, Vignette, Dehaze, and Clarity for a soft, natural warm look.

nodes.label: Convert composite to Smart Object and open Camera Raw Filter
nodes.detail: Converts the composite layer to a Smart Object and opens Filter > Camera Raw Filter to begin applying the grade non-destructively.

nodes.label: Adjust White Balance, Highlights, Shadows, and Whites/Blacks, according to Claude's suggestion, but lower the temperature and increase the highlights slightly, and confirm Camera Raw Filter
nodes.detail: Works through Temperature/Tint (skipping most of Claude's suggested warmth since the image was already warm), raises Highlights, lifts Shadows ~10-15, and reduces Blacks for added contrast.

Step 3.step_name: Create and integrate a fractal glass effect
Step 3.step_action: I will place a fractal glass texture layer over the graded composite. I will set the blending mode to Screen or Lighten to simulate realistic, in-camera prismatic light refractions interacting with the environment.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a fractal-glass blending approach
nodes.detail: Types the request 'I want to add fractal glass effect' along with having a fractal texture already made, confirmed verbatim on screen at ~18:22.

nodes.label: Outline a 8-step manual displacement-map blending approach
nodes.detail: Suggests a manual Photoshop workflow using Filter > Distort > Displace with the fractal texture saved as its own .PSD displacement map, and asks whether the effect should read as a full-surface window-pane look or a localized fracture over just part of the image.

nodes.label: Follow step 1 to create and rename the fractal glass layer
Ask to use Filter Gallery instead
nodes.detail: Follows up asking 'How about using fractal glass effect via filter gallery?', steering away from the manual displacement-map method just suggested.

nodes.label: Walk through 8-stepFilter Gallery > Glass setup
nodes.detail: Guides creating a flattened layer group renamed 'Fractal Glass', converting it to a Smart Object, and using Filter Gallery > Distort > Glass with a loaded custom texture (noting Load Texture only accepts .PSD files), in response to the Filter Gallery follow-up.

nodes.label: Apply the Glass filter and tune Distortion/Smoothness/Scaling, following Claude's suggestion for step 1, 2, 3, 5,  but slightly increase smoothness
nodes.detail: Applies the Glass filter, testing Distortion (~18), Smoothness (~7, which Claude suggested 3-5 and described as governing how 'believable' the glass looks), and Scaling (tested up toward visible texture-line gaps, settling ~90-100), producing a dramatic streaked, prismatic look.

Step 4.step_name: Add blur, grain, and hue/saturation adjustments for heightened realism
Step 4.step_action: I will apply a subtle Gaussian blur to slightly soften the digital crispness, followed by a layer of uniform film grain to optically bind the composite parts. Finally, I will use a Hue/Saturation layer to harmonize the overall color palette.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for adding blur and grain to make the glass effect over the face more real
nodes.detail: Asks Claude for a layer mask to soften the glass effect over the face.

nodes.label: Recommend a layer mask to soften the glass effect over the face
nodes.detail: Suggests adding a layer mask and painting black with a soft brush over the face/eyes at lower opacity so the glass effect reads as atmospheric rather than fully obscuring the subject.

Add grain from Filter Gallery and fine-tune it
Ask Claude for adding a slight blur to the image
Recommend adding a light Gaussian Blur (0.5-1.5px) as the final layer
Apply the Gaussian Blur

Step 5.step_name: Integrate dimensional typography using inverted masks and layer styles
Step 5.step_action: I will add a text layer, select its pixels, and apply it as an inverted layer mask to the fractal glass layer so the texture interacts uniquely with the letters. I will then add Bevel & Emboss and Drop Shadow layer styles to the text to give it a 3D, carved-out appearance.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for adding text COOL and blend it with the fractal glass effect
Provide the 8-step text workflow
nodes.detail: Lays out steps: type a text layer, Ctrl+click select its pixels, use the selection to build a mask on the Fractal Glass layer, invert it, then add Bevel & Emboss and Drop Shadow layer styles.

nodes.label: Review the steps recommended by Claude
Follow the first 4 steps to add text and apply Glass filter and fractal texture to the text
Ask Claude for blending settings for the text
nodes.detail: Asks Claude for layer-style settings to make the carved text pop.

nodes.label: Recommend Bevel & Emboss and Drop Shadow parameters
nodes.detail: Recommends a Bevel & Emboss angle around 120 with a smooth technique, and Drop Shadow settings (Multiply blend mode, opacity ~40-60%, distance ~2-4px, spread 0-5).

nodes.label: Apply text setting suggested by Claude but slightly increasing depth

Step 6.step_name: Incorporate a dynamic pixel stretch effect for a surreal, modern finish
Step 6.step_action: I will create a stamped visible layer of the current composite, then use the Single Row Marquee Tool or Single Column Marquee Tool to select a 1-pixel sliver of the subject's most prominent colors. I will duplicate this selection to a new layer and use the Free Transform tool to stretch the pixels dramatically across the canvas. Finally, I will apply a Warp transformation to give the stretched pixels a fluid, wavy motion and use a soft layer mask to tuck the effect behind the subject and typography.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a trending pixel-stretch effect
nodes.detail: Asks Claude to help add a trending pixel-stretch effect ('Help me with adding a final pixel...' confirmed on screen).

nodes.label: Web-search and recommend the single-column marquee technique
nodes.detail: Performs a live web search ('Searched the web... Found it') and recommends selecting and stretching a 1px-wide column, suggesting the strips be pulled from the glass-distorted sky area (which already carries the established color/blur/grain texture) rather than the subject, and applying the effect before any final unifying blur/grain pass.

nodes.label: Follow claude's recommendation to add the pixel stretch effect
nodes.detail: Uses Select Subject and copies the isolated subject to a new 'Subject copy' layer, flattening, stretch a 1px column with Free Transform, and adjust the opacity.
